content: Multicellular organisms are composed of more than one cell, with these cells being specialized to perform distinct functions. Most visible life forms, including all members of the kingdoms Plantae and Animalia (with exceptions like Myxozoans), are multicellular. The simplest living multicellular organisms, such as sponges, consist of various specialized cell types that work together for a shared purpose. These cell types include choanocytes, which are responsible for digestion; sclerocytes, which secrete structural support materials; porocytes, which form tubular pores; and pinacocytes, which serve as epidermal cells. While these cells collectively form a macroscopic, organized structure—the sponge—they do not form true interconnected tissues. This is evident from the fact that a sponge broken apart in a blender can reassemble itself from the surviving cells. However, individual cell types cannot survive independently if separated. In contrast, simpler colonial organisms like Volvox have cells that are free-living and capable of surviving on their own when separated from the colony. More complex organisms, such as jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones, exhibit a tissue level of organization. In these organisms, differentiated and interconnected cells work together as a group to perform specialized functions. For example, jellyfish tissues include an epidermis and a nerve net for protection and sensory functions, as well as an inner gastrodermis for digestion. The spatial organization of these differentiated cells is a subject of anatomical study. Even more complex organisms possess an organ level of development, where multiple tissues combine to form organs with specific functions. Organs can range from the primitive brain of a flatworm, which is merely a cluster of ganglion cells, to the massive stem of a sequoia tree, which can reach up to 90 meters in height, or the highly complex and multifunctional liver of vertebrates. The most advanced organisms, such as mammals, trees, and flowering plants, have organ systems in which groups of organs collaborate to perform intricate, interrelated functions. Each organ within the system focuses on a subset of tasks. For instance, in the vertebrate digestive system, the mouth and esophagus ingest food, the stomach crushes and liquefies it, the pancreas and gallbladder produce and release digestive enzymes, and the intestines absorb nutrients into the bloodstream. The development of sexual reproduction in unicellular organisms during the Ectasian period of the Mesoproterozoic era is believed to have driven the evolution and emergence of multicellular life. This is a topic of interest in developmental biology, particularly in the study of gametes such as sperm and egg cells. However, multicellular organisms also face challenges such as cancer, which arises when cells fail to regulate their growth according to the normal developmental program.
